title: Flower festival
hookLine: Hanamatsuri in Japan: flowers and sweet tea for the baby Buddha

lines: ONE HAND UP, ONE HAND DOWN.
A QUIET TURN IN AN OLD TEXT.
cards: A tiny roofed shrine covered in fresh flowers. A little statue of the baby Buddha, one hand pointing up and one pointing down, and a line of children ladling sweet tea over his head.
You've stood in this courtyard before: in your first year on this path, Hanamatsuri arrived as a new word. The flowers and the tea come back every spring.
This time, look past the scene to the old text behind it, and the quiet turn at its very end, which is easy to miss.

teach.b: The birth story the festival acts out comes from a sutta in the Majjhima Nikaya, the one on wonderful and marvelous qualities. Its setting is easy to skip.
Monks are sitting together after their meal, marveling at the Buddha's powers, when he walks in and asks what they were talking about.
He asks Ananda to say more, and Ananda recites a long list of wonders he says he heard from the Buddha's own lips. The mother gives birth standing.
The newborn stands on his own feet, takes seven steps, looks around, and declares that he is foremost in the world and this is his last birth.

teach.h: TWO STREAMS OF WATER, COOL AND WARM.
teach.b: Two streams of water, one cool and one warm, appear from the sky to bathe mother and child. That's the wonder the ladles repeat, and the flowers stand for the garden at Lumbini, where tradition places the birth.
Now the turn. When Ananda finishes, the Buddha doesn't add a louder miracle. In paraphrase, he says: then remember this too as wonderful.

teach.h: FEELINGS KNOWN AS THEY ARISE AND PASS.
teach.b: For the one who has woken up, feelings are known as they arise, as they stay, and as they pass away. So are perceptions. So are thoughts.

After all the marvels of the birth, the sutta ends on the plainest one: seeing clearly what is happening in one's own mind. That changes how the festival can look. The baby with one hand raised is where the story starts.
A child's full attention on a ladle and a thin stream of tea is closer to where the sutta ends.

how: At Hanamatsuri, temples in Japan set up a small flower-covered shrine with a statue of the newborn Buddha, and visitors ladle sweet tea over it, and some take tea home to drink.

games.q: Ananda has just recited the wonders of the birth: seven steps, two streams of water from the sky. what does the Buddha add?
o: a greater miracle from the night of his awakening
feelings, perceptions and thoughts known as they arise, stay and pass
a promise of more wonders to come
games.why: he tells Ananda to remember this too as wonderful: for the one who has woken up, feelings, perceptions and thoughts are known as they arise, stay and pass away.

practice: Hold a cup of tea or water, or picture one, and slowly, with full attention, pour a little: over a plant, into a glass, into your own palm.
Notice the sound, the weight, the way it moves, as if pouring over something new and fragile. Then set the cup down, rest your hands, and stay a moment with how careful that was.

wordCard.voice: Flower festival. Hanamatsuri, when temples in Japan cover a small shrine in flowers and people pour sweet tea over the baby Buddha, remembering his birth in the garden. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali puppha: flower. the shrine's flowers stand for the garden where the Buddha was born.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet tea. The plainest wonder is a mind seen clearly. Go gently.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 123 (Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta): the birth, seven steps, two streams of water, and the closing wonder of feelings known as they arise and pass
